articles.title: Comedy is funnier when it is easier to process, new psychology study finds
articles.summary: A new study in the Journal of Experimental Social Psychology reveals that jokes, memes, and punchlines are significantly funnier when they are easy to process. This cognitive fluency helps our brains quickly make sense of unexpected humour.

articles.title: A longer exhale may push your brain toward bolder decisions
articles.summary: Slow breathing with a prolonged exhale made people more willing to take risks by changing heart activity and increasing the brain’s sensitivity to rewards. The findings suggest that something as simple as controlling your breath can directly influence how you evaluate choices.

articles.title: Scientists reveal the hidden instructions that build the human brain
articles.summary: UCLA researchers have discovered two powerful influences that help guide how the human brain forms before birth. Radial glia, stem cells responsible for producing much of the cerebral cortex, change their behavior depending on how they process glucose and on physical contact with signals arriving from the thalamus. Those signals can alter which types of neurons are produced, including upper-layer neurons that are especially prominent in humans.

articles.title: People with unfulfilled romantic needs form stronger attachments to fictional characters
articles.summary: Singles and people unhappy in their romantic relationships are more likely to develop strong emotional and physical attractions to fictional characters, suggesting one-sided media crushes can serve as a substitute for unfulfilled real-world needs.

articles.title: Stanford scientists discover a seafood that can reverse signs of aging
articles.summary: A substance found in edible sea squirts appeared to reverse several signs of aging in older mice. Plasmalogen supplements improved memory and learning, strengthened connections between brain cells, reduced inflammation, and even helped the mice grow thicker, darker hair. Researchers believe the compounds may encourage brain regeneration and protect aging synapses.

articles.title: New injectable treatment helps the brain rebuild after stroke
articles.summary: Duke researchers developed an injectable scaffold that helped stroke-damaged brains grow new blood vessels, support nerve regrowth, and recover movement in mice. The treatment appears to work partly by recruiting the body’s own immune cells, including neutrophils that may switch from damaging to helpful under the right conditions.

articles.title: Scientists build a more accurate Alzheimer’s risk score using global DNA data
articles.summary: Standard genetic tests for Alzheimer's often fail in non-European populations. A new study shows that blending global genetic data creates a highly accurate tool that predicts both Alzheimer's risk and underlying brain damage across diverse ancestral groups.

articles.title: Personality impairments link childhood maltreatment to adult anxiety
articles.summary: A recent study finds that childhood emotional abuse and neglect are strongly linked to adult anxiety. This relationship is largely explained by impairments in how a person perceives themselves and connects with others.

articles.title: First human trial of psilocin since the 1960s reveals better tolerability than psilocybin
articles.summary: A new study suggests that consuming psilocin directly—rather than its precursor, psilocybin—provides a similar psychedelic experience with fewer side effects. Researchers also found that taking the drug under the tongue produced emotional breakthroughs despite milder effects.

articles.title: Watching violent online pornography is linked to poorer sexual health
articles.summary: Young adults who frequently watch physically violent online pornography report lower empathy, more acceptance of violence against women, and increased difficulties with sexual function, according to a large survey conducted in Spain.

articles.summary: Researchers have identified a specific brain circuit that drives increased alcohol intake following social isolation. The findings provide a biological mechanism for how a negative social environment changes what the brain treats as a valuable reward.

articles.title: Brain damage reveals how a specific region generates mind-wandering
articles.summary: Damage to the ventromedial prefrontal cortex hinders a person's ability to let their mind wander. A new small study suggests this brain region is necessary for generating the internal thoughts and memories that distract us from the present.

articles.title: Over half the risk for postpartum psychosis is tied to genetics, large study finds
articles.summary: A new study indicates that over half the risk for postpartum psychosis is driven by genetics. The findings provide evidence that the condition is a biological vulnerability rather than just a psychological reaction to childbirth.

articles.title: Singlehood is increasingly celebrated among women, but the pressure to couple up persists
articles.summary: "Single positivity" encourages young women to embrace independence, but this cultural approval comes with an expiration date. A new study reveals that as single women age, they face renewed societal pressure to settle down and find a partner.

articles.summary: While people generally prefer it when AI use in communication is openly disclosed, a new psychology study shows we heavily overestimate how much others rely on these digital assistants compared to ourselves.

articles.title: Structure and Implementation of New Practical English Textbooks Driven by Artificial Intelligence
articles.summary: arXiv:2609.02981v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Artificial intelligence is changing the form of applied English materials from fixed paper sequences to adaptive learning systems that can diagnose learners, recommend tasks, and provide formative feedback. This paper studies the structure and application of a new practical English textbook driven by artificial intelligence. A five-layer architecture is proposed: knowledge mapping, learner profiling, task generation, feedback orchestration, and teacher-side governance. A prototype was tested on 186 non-English-major undergraduates for eight weeks
